content: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a genetic disorder caused by either a homozygous deletion of the SMN1 gene on chromosome 5 or a heterozygous deletion combined with a point mutation in the second SMN1 allele. This genetic defect leads to the degeneration of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord, resulting in progressive muscle weakness. Children with SMA type I are unable to sit without support and typically either die or require full-time ventilatory support before the age of two years. Historically, there were no drug treatments available to alter the course of SMA type I. However, recent advancements have introduced potential therapeutic options, prompting an updated review of the evidence. The primary objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of drug therapies aimed at slowing or halting the progression of SMA type I. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs involving participants with clinically and genetically confirmed SMA type I. The primary outcome was the age at death or the need for full-time ventilation. Secondary outcomes included the acquisition of motor milestones (e.g., head control, rolling, sitting, or standing), motor milestone responses on disability scores within one year of treatment initiation, and adverse events related to the treatment. Two RCTs were identified. The first trial evaluated intrathecal nusinersen compared to a sham procedure in 121 infants with SMA type I. This trial was stopped early due to evidence of efficacy. After 183 days of treatment, 41% of nusinersen-treated infants demonstrated predefined improvements on the Hammersmith Infant Neurological Examination-Section 2 (HINE-2), compared to 0% in the control group. Final analyses, conducted after 6 to 13 months of treatment, showed that nusinersen reduced the risk of death or the need for full-time ventilation by 47% compared to the control group (hazard ratio 0.53, 95% confidence interval 0.32 to 0.89). Moderate-certainty evidence indicated that a greater proportion of nusinersen-treated infants achieved motor milestones, such as head control (16/73 infants), independent sitting (6/73 infants), rolling over (7/73 infants), and standing (1/73 infants), compared to the control group. Additionally, 71% of nusinersen-treated infants were classified as responders on the CHOP INTEND motor disability scale, compared to only 3% in the control group. Adverse events and serious adverse events were common in both groups but were not more frequent in the nusinersen group. The second trial compared riluzole to placebo in 10 children with SMA type I. Three of the seven children treated with riluzole survived to the ages of 30, 48, and 64 months, while all three children in the placebo group died. However, none of the children in either group achieved the ability to sit, and no adverse effects were reported. The evidence from this trial was of very low certainty due to the small sample size, baseline differences, and early termination of the study after the pharmaceutical company withdrew funding. In conclusion, intrathecal nusinersen likely prolongs survival and reduces the need for full-time ventilation in infants with SMA type I. It also increases the likelihood of achieving motor milestones and being classified as a responder on clinical assessments. The risk of adverse events with nusinersen is not higher than with a sham procedure. In contrast, the evidence for riluzole is very limited and inconclusive. Ongoing and future trials are needed to provide higher-certainty evidence, evaluate long-term outcomes, and compare new treatments to nusinersen or assess their use in combination with nusinersen.
